expectedText:
ORGAN AND BONE MARROW DONOR LEAVE — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme Corp.

LEAVE REQUEST
Jordan Lee requests organ or bone marrow donor leave from Acme Corp. as described below.

Type of donation (organ or bone marrow): _______________________________________________
Requested start date: _______________
Expected return date: _______________
Written verification of donor status and medical necessity attached: Yes / No
Whether paid statutory leave, additional unpaid organ-donation leave, or a combination is being requested: _______________________________________________

WHO THIS LEAVE APPLIES TO
California's organ and bone marrow donor leave law, codified at Labor Code §§ 1508-1513 and titled the Michelle Maykin Memorial Donation Protection Act, applies to an "employer," defined for purposes of this part as "any person, partnership, corporation, association, or other business entity that employs 15 or more employees." "Employee" and "employee benefits" carry the same meanings given those terms in Labor Code § 1501, a different statute in this same code that this clause does not independently analyze.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Employer” means any person, partnership, corporation, association, or other business entity that employs 15 or more employees."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1509(b) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1509(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1509.)
  "“Employee” and “employee benefits” have the same meanings set forth in Section 1501."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1509(a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1509(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1509.)
  Known gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own organ and bone marrow donor leave coverage threshold — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific workplace, and not a comparison to any other leave law's own coverage threshold (this corpus's separate FMLA and CFRA documents describe those laws' own, different thresholds). Both citations here are subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 1509 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — not two independent sources. This clause does not itself state or cross-reference the definitions actually found at Labor Code § 1501; it reports only that § 1509 borrows them by reference. This document is informational: it does not determine whether any specific employer meets or falls short of the 15-employee threshold.

THE LEAVE ENTITLEMENT
Subject to a written-verification requirement described elsewhere in this statute, a covered employer must grant a covered employee two distinct paid leaves. The first: "A leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person." The second: "A leave of absence, not exceeding five business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is a bone marrow donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s bone marrow to another person." Beyond that paid organ-donation leave, the statute separately requires the employer to grant an additional unpaid leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person. In each instance, the one-year period is measured from the date the employee’s leave begins and consists of 12 consecutive months.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1510(a)(1) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1510.)
  "A leave of absence, not exceeding five business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is a bone marrow donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s bone marrow to another person."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(a)(2) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1510(a)(2) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1510.)
  "an employer shall grant an additional unpaid leave of absence, not exceeding 30 business days in a one-year period, to an employee who is an organ donor, for the purpose of donating the employee’s organ to another person."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(b) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1510(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1510.)
  Known gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of the specific day-amounts and paid/unpaid character of California's organ and bone marrow donor leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific leave, and not a claim that a particular employee currently qualifies. All three citations here are subdivisions of one statutory section, § 1510 (subdivisions (a)(1), (a)(2), and (b)) — not three independent sources. This clause does not address the separate written-verification/medical-necessity condition on receiving this leave, the separate rule against running this leave concurrently with FMLA or CFRA leave, or the separate rule letting an employer require use of accrued sick leave, vacation, or paid time off as a condition of the leave's initial receipt — each addressed in other clauses. Nor does it address whether or how the 30-business-day paid organ leave and the additional 30-business-day unpaid organ leave interact with each other in practice; the statute states them as two distinct grants without further elaboration in the text quoted here.

VERIFICATION AND USE OF ACCRUED LEAVE
To receive either the paid organ or bone marrow donation leave, or the additional unpaid organ donation leave, described in this statute, an employee "shall provide written verification to the employer that the employee is an organ or bone marrow donor and that there is a medical necessity for the donation of the organ or bone marrow." Separately, the statute allows an employer to require, as a condition of an employee's initial receipt of bone marrow or organ donation leave, that the employee first use a stated amount of earned but unused paid leave: "up to five days of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for bone marrow donation and up to two weeks of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for organ donation, unless doing so would violate the provisions of any applicable collective bargaining agreement."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "In order to receive a leave of absence pursuant to subdivision (a) or (b) an employee shall provide written verification to the employer that the employee is an organ or bone marrow donor and that there is a medical necessity for the donation of the organ or bone marrow."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(c) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1510(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1510.)
  "An employer may require, as a condition of an employee’s initial receipt of bone marrow or organ donation leave, that an employee take up to five days of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for bone marrow donation and up to two weeks of earned but unused sick leave, vacation, or paid time off for organ donation, unless doing so would violate the provisions of any applicable collective bargaining agreement."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(g) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1510(g) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1510.)
  Known gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own written-verification condition and its own accrued-leave-use option for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific request, and not a description of any particular employer's actual verification form or practice. Both citations here are subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 1510 (subdivisions (c) and (g)) — not two independent sources. The statute's own text does not specify who must supply the written verification (the employee's own statement, a treating or transplant physician, or some other source) or what "medical necessity" documentation must contain beyond the quoted language; this clause does not fill that gap. This clause also does not address whether an employer that requires use of accrued leave under subdivision (g) must still separately pay the statutory 30-business-day organ or five-business-day bone marrow leave described elsewhere once accrued leave is exhausted; the statute states both provisions without describing how they offset against each other beyond the caps quoted here.

RELATIONSHIP TO FMLA AND CFRA LEAVE
This statute states its own, separate rule for how organ and bone marrow donation leave relates to leave taken under the federal Family and Medical Leave Act or California's own family-leave statute: "Notwithstanding existing law, bone marrow and organ donation leave shall not be taken concurrently with any leave taken pursuant to the federal Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.) or the Moore-Brown-Roberti Family Rights Act (Sections 12945.2 and 19702.3 of the Government Code)." The statute names the California Family Rights Act by its formal statutory title, the Moore-Brown-Roberti Family Rights Act, and cites it as Government Code §§ 12945.2 and 19702.3.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding existing law, bone marrow and organ donation leave shall not be taken concurrently with any leave taken pursuant to the federal Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993 (29 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.) or the Moore-Brown-Roberti Family Rights Act (Sections 12945.2 and 19702.3 of the Government Code)."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1510(h) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1510(h) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1510.)
  Known gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own no-concurrent-running rule for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific case, and not a restatement of the separate rule (found in a different statute) describing how FMLA and CFRA leave run together with each other. This corpus's own, separate CFRA document describes that different concurrency rule between FMLA and CFRA; this clause addresses only organ/bone marrow donation leave's relationship to those two other leaves, not their relationship to each other. This clause quotes a single subdivision of a single statutory section, § 1510(h); no additional independent source was found for this specific rule. The statute's own text does not further explain the mechanical consequence of "shall not be taken concurrently" — for example, whether it means the leaves must be taken in sequence, or only that time on one leave is not counted against the days available under the other; this clause reports the statute's own words without resolving that question.

REINSTATEMENT AFTER LEAVE
On the expiration of leave taken under this statute, the employer's reinstatement obligation is stated as follows: "An employer shall, upon expiration of a leave authorized by this part, restore an employee to the position held by him or her when the leave began or to a position with equivalent seniority status, employee benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment." That obligation has a stated limit: "An employer may decline to restore an employee as required in this section because of conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part by the employee."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer shall, upon expiration of a leave authorized by this part, restore an employee to the position held by him or her when the leave began or to a position with equivalent seniority status, employee benefits, pay, and other terms and conditions of employment."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1511 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1511 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1511.)
  "An employer may decline to restore an employee as required in this section because of conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part by the employee."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1511 (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1511 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1511.)
  Known gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own reinstatement rule for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific reinstatement decision, and not a claim that any particular employer's stated reason for declining to restore an employee is, or is not, "unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part." This clause quotes the two sentences of a single statutory section, § 1511, in full; no additional independent source was found for this rule. The statute does not define "conditions unrelated to the exercise of rights under this part" beyond that phrase itself, and this clause does not attempt to define it further. Separately, Labor Code § 1510(d) — not quoted in this clause — addresses continuity of service and, during paid organ-donation leave, continued group health plan coverage; this clause does not restate that provision.

PROTECTION AGAINST INTERFERENCE AND RETALIATION
This statute states its own, separate prohibitions on interference and retaliation. On interference: "An employer shall not interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise or the attempt to exercise a right established by this part." On retaliation: "An employer shall not discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee who does either of the following: (1) Exercises a right provided under this part. (2) Opposes a practice made unlawful by this part."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer shall not interfere with, restrain, or deny the exercise or the attempt to exercise a right established by this part."
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1512(a) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1512(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1512.)
  "An employer shall not discharge, fine, suspend, expel, discipline, or in any other manner discriminate against an employee who does either of the following"
  — Cal. Lab. Code § 1512(b) (California Legislative Information text), Lab. C. § 1512(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=1512.)
  Known gap: This is one state statute, used as evidence of California's own interference and anti-retaliation rules for this specific leave — not a claim about which state's law governs a specific dispute, and not a claim that any specific employer action against any specific employee did or did not violate this statute. Both citations here are subdivisions of a single statutory section, § 1512 (subdivisions (a) and (b)) — not two independent sources. This clause does not describe the separate enforcement mechanism the same statutory part provides — Labor Code § 1513, not quoted here, allows an employee to bring a civil action in superior court and lets the court order equitable relief — nor any deadline, damages, or procedure that might apply to such an action.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to acknowledge this leave request and the terms above.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
